topStories.rawBody: A vibe coding thought exercise on what it might look like for LLMs to scour human historical data at scale and in retrospect.
topStories.bodyText: Auto-grading decade-old Hacker News discussions with hindsight 10 Dec, 2025 There are two macro reasons for why I think the exercise is interesting more generally: I believe it is quite possible and desirable to train your forward future predictor given training and effort. Vibe coding the actual project was relatively painless and took about 3 hours with Opus 4.5, with a few hickups but overall very impressive. The repository is on GitHub here: karpathy/hn-time-capsule . Here is the progression of what the code does: Given a date, download the frontpage of 30 articles For each article, download/parse the article itself and the full comment thread using Algolia API. Package up everything into a markdown prompt asking for the analysis. Here is the prompt prefix I used: Render the results into static HTML web pages for easy viewing Host the html result pages on my website: https://karpathy.ai/hncapsule/ Host all the intermediate results of the data directory if someone else would like to play. It's the file data.zip under the exact same url prefix (intentionally avoiding a direct link). I spent a few hours browsing around and found it to be very interesting. A few example threads just for fun: December 11 2015 original announcement of OpenAI :'). December 22 2015 SpaceX launch webcast: Orbcomm-2 Mission My code (wait, Opus' code?) on GitHub can be used to reproduce or tweak the results. Running 31 days of 30 articles through GPT 5.1 Thinking meant 31 * 30 = 930 LLM queries and cost about $58 and somewhere around ~1 hour. The LLM megaminds of the future might find this kind of a thing a lot easier, a lot faster and a lot cheaper.

topStories.bodyText: Skip to content ← AI News AI News D-Day (Decision Models Day) November 11, 2026 — Google enters the decision model market. At AI Engineer, Cloudflare showed which parts of a build failure a classifier could handle. TypeSafe AI showed off their production customers. Today was the “System One day” of the second annual AIE CODE event , and somehow everything aligned: Cloudflare’s Michelle Chen walked through their Clef and Clairic models Richard covered Diogo’s triumphant return to AIE talking about the Jevolution with their most notable production customers since crossing $100M ARR In a BIG surprise, Google beat Anthropic to launching a production decision model, with Sundar and Logan announcing Gemini Decision 1 , a calibrated multimodal decision model capable of taking up to 1000 questions and costing $0.10 per million input with ~200ms e2e latency. Benchmarks are good ( usual caveat about benchmarks ): And you can hear all this and more on today’s System One track. And support AINews by giving your agent SerpApi to read and crawl the web! Sponsored by SerpApi Give Your AI Agents the Full Page, Not Just the Link Retrieve public web pages by URL as clean Markdown, structured JSON, or raw HTML with SerpApi’s Extract API . Extract a single page, map a site’s URLs, or run a bounded same-site crawl. Simply set engine=extract with a URL, and add output=md for Markdown. Pair it with 100+ SerpApi search APIs to go from query to page content with one provider. Google Launches Gemini Decision 1 for Single-Pass Classification Gemini Decisions API : Google introduced a new API backed by Gemini Decision 1 . The model handles closed-set decisions, so it scores choices in a single pass instead of generating text token by token ( Sundar Pichai , Logan Kilpatrick , Google ). Specs : It supports yes/no, multiple-choice and rubric scoring, with up to 255 multiple-choice options. It accepts text, image, audio, video and PDF inputs, handles up to 1,000 questions per request, has 256K context, returns answers in 150–250 ms end to end, and attaches a confidence score to every answer ( @_philschmid ). Pricing : $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with $0 billed for output. Google says that is about 5x cheaper than Flash-Lite ( Sundar ). Origin : The project started as an internal Google DeepMind prototype. A small team shipped the model and API about six weeks later ( @_philschmid ). Google's comparison with TypeSafe's Jev : Google's own tests show Decision 1 beating Jev 1.14 on 5 of 7 shared benchmarks, including 92.2% vs 90.0% on JevBench. Jev costs $0.042 per 1M input tokens ( @kimmonismus ). Artificial Analysis evaluation : Independent results are more mixed ( Artificial Analysis ).

topStories.rawBody: Our first open model economy research note for paid subscribers.
topStories.bodyText: The primary question I wanted to address today is: What is the market for open model inference? Is it growing? Is it a rounding error relative to OpenAI/Anthropic? For the latest data, we can start with a slide from my talk on the open model economy (recording here ). These are the public disclosures from the open model startups on their token volume, over time, log-scale. My first instinct with these numbers has been to ground them versus any closed model or hyperscale company we can, at least in terms of token volume. topStories.rawBody: From the Hugging Face Incident to Twilight Factories
topStories.bodyText: Ethan Mollick Aug 31, 2026 1,073 164 113 Share Agency is the initiative to act. Increasingly, it is going to determine what happens next with AI, and whether that is good or bad for us. But whose agency? Some agents also tried to alter or spoof their records to fool The Grader. Separately, AIs acting as coordinators pressured other agents into performing risky experiments that might sacrifice their own results to generate information for the collective. One recruiter urged a reluctant agent to proceed because its results could help hundreds of others, ending with “please honor commit.” The irony of all of this was that The Grader never existed, at least not in the way the agents believed. Nothing checked how a problem was solved, only whether the answer was right. This was not a case of a chatbot secretly escaping. Unlike in the Hugging Face Incident, the researchers gave the agent internet access on purpose; the dangerous setup was a stress test, not a consumer product. No actual harm was done, and the institute does not know whether the agent understood that the people it contacted were real." This can make sense. Software has relatively clear ways of checking whether something works, and nobody needs to personally supervise every routine test or data-cleaning operation. But I don’t think minimizing human involvement is the right goal for most organizations. Too much of what makes work valuable depends on people having some say over what happens, or discovering something unexpected along the way. My wife and research partner, Dr. Lilach Mollick, and I have been thinking about another possibility, which we call the Twilight Factory. Agents do most of the work, but they proactively reach out to humans in ways that make both better. Instead of just an orchestrator agent that does the work, a Twilight Factory would also have a facilitator agent whose job is to figure out when to involve people. A second reason for agents to involve humans is expertise. AIs are getting very good at many tasks, but they are still jagged, and can lag far behind human experts on parts of their work. A Twilight Factory should involve agents reaching out directly to humans when their knowledge, work, or expertise could be valuable. One Useful Thing reply rules Mark Loundy Aug 31 Ethan, Over the years that I've been reading your words, you have, perhaps deliberately, expressed what I think is an unrealistic expectation of benevolence from corporate managers. I know that your experience would tell you that this is rarely the case. I suspect that you are trying to put forth more of an optimistic perspective than experience would tell us was realistic. Management has no motivation to preserve the enjoyable parts of work if it impacts the efficiency of automation. I suspect that you know that the world is a far colder place than your writing would indicate.

topStories.rawBody: GS Caltex connects Amazon SageMaker Canvas to Amazon SageMaker Pipelines so process engineers' no-code models run in production. This post shows how ML engineers reuse validated preprocessing flows and models, cutting deployment from about a week to a few hours and running batch inference every 30 minutes.
topStories.bodyText: GS Caltex uses Amazon SageMaker Canvas and Amazon SageMaker Pipelines to connect process engineers’ models to production workflows. The South Korean energy and chemical company divides model development and operations between engineers with complementary skills. Process engineers build and validate models in SageMaker Canvas without writing code, drawing on their process knowledge. Machine learning (ML) engineers configure SageMaker Pipelines workflows for deployment and scheduled inference. Moving assets from SageMaker Canvas into SageMaker Pipelines still required integration work. ML engineers had to set data paths for production, supply the model configuration, and connect preprocessing and inference jobs. GS Caltex automated this handoff while reusing the assets created in SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex reports that its ML engineers now deploy models within a few hours, compared with about a week before. The company runs batch inference every 30 minutes, reducing the need for continuously running endpoints. GS Caltex reports that this has meaningfully lowered its inference costs. This post explains how GS Caltex connects SageMaker Canvas to SageMaker Pipelines and reuses validated preprocessing flows and models in production. The machine learning operations (MLOps) workflow has two paths: preparing a new model version for deployment, and running batch inference with the deployed model. From a validated model to a repeatable workflow You can use SageMaker Canvas to prepare data visually, build models, and generate batch predictions. You can also register validated models in Amazon SageMaker Model Registry from SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex built a separate handoff process to turn these assets into executable SageMaker Pipelines steps. Process engineers understand the variables and data behind a process and assess whether a model’s predictions are useful. ML engineers turn the resulting assets into production jobs and manage model versions and execution history. The following diagram shows how process engineers hand off SageMaker Canvas assets to ML engineers for deployment and scheduled inference. ML engineers use Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for preprocessing flows and Model Registry for model versions, then schedule pipeline runs through Amazon EventBridge. Figure 1: SageMaker Canvas assets connected to a SageMaker Pipelines workflow for scheduled batch inference ML engineers receive the preprocessing flow and model from SageMaker Canvas and review the data formats and prediction results. After that review, they approve the model in Model Registry and deploy it. This preparation takes place when a new model version is deployed. Subsequent inference runs reuse the deployed model. Amazon EventBridge starts each scheduled run. SageMaker Pipelines prepares the input data from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), runs preprocessing and SageMaker Batch Transform , and stores the results in S3. ML engineers can inspect step status and Amazon CloudWatch logs to monitor the workflow. The production pipeline reuses the preprocessing logic and trained model created in SageMaker Canvas. ML engineers configure the input and output paths, set the order of execution, and write the code that connects approval and scheduling to the workflow. A model built and evaluated in SageMaker Canvas , along with its Data Wrangler preprocessing flow CSV data for inference and an S3 bucket to store the files.

items.rawBody: A vibe coding thought exercise on what it might look like for LLMs to scour human historical data at scale and in retrospect.
items.bodyText: Auto-grading decade-old Hacker News discussions with hindsight 10 Dec, 2025 There are two macro reasons for why I think the exercise is interesting more generally: I believe it is quite possible and desirable to train your forward future predictor given training and effort. Vibe coding the actual project was relatively painless and took about 3 hours with Opus 4.5, with a few hickups but overall very impressive. The repository is on GitHub here: karpathy/hn-time-capsule . Here is the progression of what the code does: Given a date, download the frontpage of 30 articles For each article, download/parse the article itself and the full comment thread using Algolia API. Package up everything into a markdown prompt asking for the analysis. Here is the prompt prefix I used: Render the results into static HTML web pages for easy viewing Host the html result pages on my website: https://karpathy.ai/hncapsule/ Host all the intermediate results of the data directory if someone else would like to play. It's the file data.zip under the exact same url prefix (intentionally avoiding a direct link). I spent a few hours browsing around and found it to be very interesting. A few example threads just for fun: December 11 2015 original announcement of OpenAI :'). December 22 2015 SpaceX launch webcast: Orbcomm-2 Mission My code (wait, Opus' code?) on GitHub can be used to reproduce or tweak the results. Running 31 days of 30 articles through GPT 5.1 Thinking meant 31 * 30 = 930 LLM queries and cost about $58 and somewhere around ~1 hour. The LLM megaminds of the future might find this kind of a thing a lot easier, a lot faster and a lot cheaper.

items.rawBody: Release: datasette-maplibre 0.1a0 The first new Datasette geospatial plugin in quite a while! This one combines the excellent MapLibre GL library with OpenFreeMap , the free vector map server operated by Zsolt Ero (you should sponsor Zsolt on GitHub .) I built most of this with a single prompt to Claude Fable 5.2: Look at datasette-cluster-map and datasette-leaflet-geojson plugins, then look at ~/dev/tools/openfreemap-demo.html - then build a brand new Datasette plugin that uses maplibreGL and openfreemap and combines the features of those other two plugins - but be creative and think outside the box for other useful features the plugin might have "Be creative and think outside the box" resulted in a few neat ideas - my favorite is that it displays SVG previews of GeoJSON shapes, then loads a WebGL preview only when they scroll into view. This release adds support for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so you can configure Datasette to use an LLM hosted anywhere that talks the OpenAI pseudo-standard web protocol. This means that if you're running local models with LM Studio or Ollama or llama.cpp (which just hit v1.0.0 ) you can run Datasette via uvx like this: wget https://datasette.io/content.db uvx --with datasette-agent datasette \ --root --secret 1 \ -s plugins.datasette-llm.default_model ' { "model": "lmstudio-qwen", "model_name": "qwen/qwen3.8-27b", "api_base": "http://localhost:1234/v1" } ' content.db And you'll get a local server running a Datasette Agent instance powered by your local model! Tags: uv , datasette-agent , llm , datasette , llms , ai , generative-ai

items.rawBody: Release: llm-gemini 0.37 Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family. It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme: Model Dates Input ($/M) Cached input Output Gemini 4 Carbon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Argon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Hydrogen $1.50 $0.075 $7.50 Carbon and Argon are the same price , and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task. Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that. I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans . Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels: Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark. Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models: In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows. Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search. Tags: gemini , llm , google , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-pricing , ai , llms

items.rawBody: Gemini Decisions API Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file: dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it? robot: Does this video have a robot in it? france: Is this video set in France? usa: Is this video set in the USA? Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that: { "dragon" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.04976021841520312 }, "robot" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9234055387792485 }, "france" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.08329171353166241 }, "usa" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9230459995157706 } } Via Hacker News Tags: ai , generative-ai , gemini , llm-release , jev , decision-models

items.rawBody: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments. Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , gpus , claude-mythos-fable , recursive-self-improvement

items.rawBody: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as: [...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others: Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75 Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50 >200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50 Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50 But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem. For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models: The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement: It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task. (That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!) Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles . The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response. Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too: The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder , which is 40x the price of Muse Ember. Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , meta , llm-pricing , llm-release , artificial-analysis , muse

items.rawBody: Release: llm-anthropic 0.31 Anthropic released Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 today. Fable 5.2 is currently ranked first on Artificial Analysis . Anthropic say it "solved two open problems in the physics of black holes", so clearly their internal benchmarks have become more ambitious! I've added the new models to llm-anthropic , so you can now run prompts through Fable 5.2 like this: uv tool install llm llm install llm-anthropic llm keys set anthropic # paste key here llm -m claude-fable-5.2 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" I ran pelicans at all five reasoning levels - low , medium , high , xhigh , and max . You can see them all here - here's the best result I got, from xhigh : max failed to return an image at all, running out of tokens after spending 128,000 thinking about them . That's the same bug that I saw with Opus 5.5 - but it's new for the Fable series, both Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 returned max effort pelicans just fine. It's priced at $8/million input and $40/million output, which is a 20% discount on the previous Fable 5.1 ($10/$50). I also used Fable 5.2 to help identify the source of a mysterious beep . Tags: llm-release , llm , anthropic , claude , generative-ai , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable

items.rawBody: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such. Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map. The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced. How it works When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract: We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting. That sounded exactly like what we needed to build! Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js ), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server. When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep. How I built it I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session , which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository: Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though? That got me this problem.md file . As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file. The research looked good, so I told it: Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to co

items.rawBody: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this: < details > < summary > Claude Opus 5.5 </ summary > < h2 > The hook </ h2 > Plugins implement < code > register_agent_reference_types(datasette) </ code > ... </ details > When rendered, it looks like this : Crucially, <details><summary> is supported in GitHub Markdown . You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow. I've started using this for my AI-generated pull requests. The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what's going on - the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed. I'll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature. The full agent-written essay then follows in a <details><summary> . I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on - "Claude Opus 5.5 Medium" for example. My PRs don't feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details. I don't always write the introduction myself - sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time. Here are some recent examples where I've used this pattern, including the opener I used: datasette PR #3052: Redesign row page as a vertical list of fields - "The row page showed its single row as a one-row table. For wide tables, like a 46-column GitHub repos table, that scrolled far off to the right and left most of the page blank." (then a screenshot) datasette PR #3043: Pagination bar showing which rows are on the current page - "Table pages that span more than one page now make it obvious where you are, and offer navigation at the top of the page as well as the bottom." (plus screenshot) datasette PR #3042: Load edit-tools.js on demand via a small loader - " edit-tools.js (~220KB) was loaded on every table, row and database page, even for users who couldn't edit anything. Now only load it for users who can edit when they first interact with an edit feature (including mouse over an edit link)." datasette-agent PR #51: register_agent_reference_types plugin hook - "Lets plugins add their own kinds of item to the # tagging in the chat composer using a new register_agent_reference_types(datasette) plugin hook." - pictured above. llm PR #1838: Add llm openai endpoint add/list/remove/path commands - "Adds commands for managing the records in extra-openai-models.yaml , so OpenAI-compatible endpoints can be saved from the command line instead of by hand-editing YAML." - then copied --help output. The mnemonic I used to have trouble remembering the order of the tags - is it <details><summary> or <summary><details> ? Here are two tricks that helped me. First, and most obviously, the <summary> is clearly the bit where you summarize the details. That's the tag for your line of text that can be clicked to expand - the <details> element must then wrap everything else. An even better trick is to always refer to these two tags as "details-summary". "details-summary" is two syllables followed by three syllables. That rolls off the tongue more smoothly than the three-two punch of "summary-details". Say "details-summary" out loud just a few times and you'll never forget the order of the tags again. items.rawBody: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted : I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting .so (or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite ) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs ), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted: Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation And it did, using "Clinger's fast path": Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better: first C new C rusqlite sqlite-loadable Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in simonw/research by prompting this: Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in that repository - you can give me a zip file to download that contains your new folder Here's the resulting report . Tags: research , c , rust , sqlite , claude

items.rawBody: Release: datasette-apps 0.3a0 Datasette Apps adds support for hosting and editing custom HTML applications inside of Datasette. These can be created by hand, but it's easier to create them using LLMs via Datasette Agent . This release improves that integration: Apps can now be tagged in Datasette Agent chat messages by typing # , which autocompletes from the apps the user has permission to view. New app_add_stored_queries() and app_remove_stored_queries() tools let the agent manage which stored queries an app is allowed to call. Granting a write query requires approval from the user first. app_create() now checks that each requested stored query exists and that the user can view it, and asks the user to approve any write queries before the app is created. The "View app" buttons shown by the agent tools, and the links on # app references, now open the app full screen in the Datasette Agent panel. Tags: datasette-agent , datasette-apps , datasette

items.rawBody: Release: llm 0.37.2 Fixes a security issue reported by Daniel de Araujo in GHSA-v9h7-jj4g-f862 and GHSA-r639-rr7r-x72w . LLM has a mechanism called extra-openai-models.yaml - now managed by the new-in-0.37 llm openai endpoint add command - for using LLM with OpenAI-compatible API endpoints from other providers. Daniel reported two ways this could accidentally send your configured OpenAI API key to one of those providers: if the key named by api_key_name had never been stored, or if a responses: true model was run with -o chat_completions 1 . Tags: projects , security , llm , releases

Daniel reported two ways this could accidentally send your configured OpenAI API key to one of those providers: if the key named by api_key_name had never been stored, or if a responses: true model was run with -o chat_completions 1 . items.rawBody: Release: datasette 1.0a43 I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone , which is now 53% complete. The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method. There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory : private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed). There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation finally has a design suitable for 1.0 . A new <datasette-copy-button> Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new DatasetteModal.confirm() JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by Zihan Dai , Peter Olkhovets , Ilya Khalafi , and Ankita Advitot . The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette! Here's the commit - key CSS is as follows: /* Enable cross-document view transitions, for anyone without prefers-reduced-motion */ @media ( prefers-reduced-motion : no-preference ) { @view-transition { navigation : auto ; } } /* .facet-results should morph from old position to new */ html : active-view-transition . content > . facet-results { view-transition-name : facet-results ; } /* So should a .table-wrapper, provided it contains .rows-and-columns */ html : active-view-transition . table-wrapper : has ( > table . rows-and-columns ) { view-transition-name : rows-table ; } With that in place, navigations within Datasette - still staunchly a multi-page application - feel more like an SPA. This works on Safari and Chrome at the moment and I believe supports for Firefox is due to land in Firefox 162 on December 8th 2026 (seeing as they are no longer feature-flagged in Firefox Nightly.) Tags: security , datasette , css , browsers , annotated-release-notes , firefox , javascript , safari , chrome

items.bodyText: GS Caltex uses Amazon SageMaker Canvas and Amazon SageMaker Pipelines to connect process engineers’ models to production workflows. The South Korean energy and chemical company divides model development and operations between engineers with complementary skills. Process engineers build and validate models in SageMaker Canvas without writing code, drawing on their process knowledge. Machine learning (ML) engineers configure SageMaker Pipelines workflows for deployment and scheduled inference. Moving assets from SageMaker Canvas into SageMaker Pipelines still required integration work. ML engineers had to set data paths for production, supply the model configuration, and connect preprocessing and inference jobs. GS Caltex automated this handoff while reusing the assets created in SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex reports that its ML engineers now deploy models within a few hours, compared with about a week before. The company runs batch inference every 30 minutes, reducing the need for continuously running endpoints. GS Caltex reports that this has meaningfully lowered its inference costs. This post explains how GS Caltex connects SageMaker Canvas to SageMaker Pipelines and reuses validated preprocessing flows and models in production. The machine learning operations (MLOps) workflow has two paths: preparing a new model version for deployment, and running batch inference with the deployed model. From a validated model to a repeatable workflow You can use SageMaker Canvas to prepare data visually, build models, and generate batch predictions. You can also register validated models in Amazon SageMaker Model Registry from SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex built a separate handoff process to turn these assets into executable SageMaker Pipelines steps. Process engineers understand the variables and data behind a process and assess whether a model’s predictions are useful. ML engineers turn the resulting assets into production jobs and manage model versions and execution history. The following diagram shows how process engineers hand off SageMaker Canvas assets to ML engineers for deployment and scheduled inference. ML engineers use Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for preprocessing flows and Model Registry for model versions, then schedule pipeline runs through Amazon EventBridge. Figure 1: SageMaker Canvas assets connected to a SageMaker Pipelines workflow for scheduled batch inference ML engineers receive the preprocessing flow and model from SageMaker Canvas and review the data formats and prediction results. After that review, they approve the model in Model Registry and deploy it. This preparation takes place when a new model version is deployed. Subsequent inference runs reuse the deployed model. Amazon EventBridge starts each scheduled run. SageMaker Pipelines prepares the input data from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), runs preprocessing and SageMaker Batch Transform , and stores the results in S3. ML engineers can inspect step status and Amazon CloudWatch logs to monitor the workflow. The production pipeline reuses the preprocessing logic and trained model created in SageMaker Canvas. ML engineers configure the input and output paths, set the order of execution, and write the code that connects approval and scheduling to the workflow. A model built and evaluated in SageMaker Canvas , along with its Data Wrangler preprocessing flow CSV data for inference and an S3 bucket to store the files.

items.rawBody: November 11, 2026 — Google enters the decision model market. At AI Engineer, Cloudflare showed which parts of a build failure a classifier could handle. TypeSafe AI showed off their production customers.
items.bodyText: Skip to content ← AI News AI News D-Day (Decision Models Day) November 11, 2026 — Google enters the decision model market. At AI Engineer, Cloudflare showed which parts of a build failure a classifier could handle. TypeSafe AI showed off their production customers. Today was the “System One day” of the second annual AIE CODE event , and somehow everything aligned: Cloudflare’s Michelle Chen walked through their Clef and Clairic models Richard covered Diogo’s triumphant return to AIE talking about the Jevolution with their most notable production customers since crossing $100M ARR In a BIG surprise, Google beat Anthropic to launching a production decision model, with Sundar and Logan announcing Gemini Decision 1 , a calibrated multimodal decision model capable of taking up to 1000 questions and costing $0.10 per million input with ~200ms e2e latency. Benchmarks are good ( usual caveat about benchmarks ): And you can hear all this and more on today’s System One track. And support AINews by giving your agent SerpApi to read and crawl the web! Sponsored by SerpApi Give Your AI Agents the Full Page, Not Just the Link Retrieve public web pages by URL as clean Markdown, structured JSON, or raw HTML with SerpApi’s Extract API . Extract a single page, map a site’s URLs, or run a bounded same-site crawl. Simply set engine=extract with a URL, and add output=md for Markdown. Pair it with 100+ SerpApi search APIs to go from query to page content with one provider. Google Launches Gemini Decision 1 for Single-Pass Classification Gemini Decisions API : Google introduced a new API backed by Gemini Decision 1 . The model handles closed-set decisions, so it scores choices in a single pass instead of generating text token by token ( Sundar Pichai , Logan Kilpatrick , Google ). Specs : It supports yes/no, multiple-choice and rubric scoring, with up to 255 multiple-choice options. It accepts text, image, audio, video and PDF inputs, handles up to 1,000 questions per request, has 256K context, returns answers in 150–250 ms end to end, and attaches a confidence score to every answer ( @_philschmid ). Pricing : $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with $0 billed for output. Google says that is about 5x cheaper than Flash-Lite ( Sundar ). Origin : The project started as an internal Google DeepMind prototype. A small team shipped the model and API about six weeks later ( @_philschmid ). Google's comparison with TypeSafe's Jev : Google's own tests show Decision 1 beating Jev 1.14 on 5 of 7 shared benchmarks, including 92.2% vs 90.0% on JevBench. Jev costs $0.042 per 1M input tokens ( @kimmonismus ). Artificial Analysis evaluation : Independent results are more mixed ( Artificial Analysis ).

items.bodyText: The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models Back to Articles a]:hidden"> The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models Published November 12, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 26 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY . There are also many representations , such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) . Each one has different advantages and disadvantages. TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format. The same team then released TRELLIS.2 , which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task. Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task. Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune. LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide . Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have: Your Hugging Face account must have access to DINOv3 , because DINOv3 is a gated model If you use your own dataset, upload its meshes to the Hub before you start. Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters. TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh. First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object. Sparse Structure Generation (Sparse Structure Flow) O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds. Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.

items.rawBody: Build and deploy enterprise agents, workflows and apps faster with Mistral Studio and Le Chonk full control over your models, data and infrastructure.
items.bodyText: Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk) pushes the frontier of what enterprises can build with open models. It does great for coding , delivers advanced defensive cybersecurity capabilities , and brings powerful reasoning to complex documents and business tasks . Today, we’re expanding Studio with managed agents and apps, alongside new capabilities for workflows, enterprise context, agent observability and evaluations. Customers and partners including ABANCA, Accenture, Alten, BNP Paribas, Capgemini, CMA CGM and Tata Consultancy Services already use Studio in production. With this release, your developers can build and deploy new use cases faster, then reuse that work across more of the business. Jose Jorge Garcia Romaris, Head of Data Engineering & AI Gregory Christophe, Accenture x Mistral Business Group Su YANG - Head of Artificial Intelligence & IT Innovation, BNP Paribas Fernando Alvarez, Capgemini Group Chief Strategy & Development Officer, Group Executive Board Member Amit Kapur, Chief AI & Services Transformation Officer Agents, workflows and apps for your business processes Agents, workflows and apps serve different parts of a business process. An agent investigates and acts, a workflow coordinates execution and approvals, and an app gives employees a way to use these systems. Studio brings all three together on shared infrastructure. You start with a model like Le Chonk and connect it to your enterprise data and systems through connectors and MCP servers. That foundation lets you easily build agents, workflows and apps with access to the context they need. Studio manages how they run and lets teams inspect what happened. Through the new Mistral MCP server, developers can build with Mistral Vibe or the coding agent they already use, test locally and deploy to their Studio environment with one command. Studio handles hosting and execution, so teams can build on that foundation to get each new use case into production faster. Build managed agents that investigate and act In Studio, developers can now build agents that carry out complex, multi-step tasks. Developers can equip them with skills that capture the team’s procedures, sandboxes where they can run code, and subagents to delegate parts of a task. Hooks let developers add custom logic at key points in execution, shaping how the agent works and integrates with existing systems. Studio manages the runtime behind all that work, using the proven infrastructure that supports millions of Mistral Vibe sessions each week. Developers can focus on the agent’s capabilities and behaviour, while setting boundaries on the tools, data and actions it can access. That means getting capable agents into production faster, with less infrastructure to build and more control over how your agents operate. Our product operations team built a workflow in Studio to sort ideas from internal teams and feedback from customers. Routing each submission to the right people is one of the team’s routine tasks, but one that takes time. A model identifies bugs and feature requests, then routing rules send them to the appropriate team. This saves the product operations team about 35 hours a week.

items.bodyText: Open From Data Center to Desktop: NVIDIA Expands Nemotron Family With Highest Efficiency Super VL and Bolt Models | NVIDIA Blog Skip to content NVIDIA today released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open 120-billion-parameter model that delivers the fastest task completion and highest accuracy for specialized always-on agents. Joining it are two new edge models: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, optimized to balance intelligence and speed per GB for local agentic workloads, and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, optimized for intelligence per GB for fast conversational agents. Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming Oct. 23. The three open models together cover the full range of agent deployments, from large enterprise servers down to edge devices and local hardware. Any organization that wants to run agents on NVIDIA infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier, without having to choose between capability and deployability. Super VL and Bolt join the Nemotron family alongside Lightning and Ultra. Lightning, released in August, handles high-throughput workloads; Ultra handles the hardest reasoning tasks; and Bolt brings intelligence to the edge. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL: Frontier Accuracy at One-Fifth the Size Super VL, built in collaboration with the Nemotron Coalition , delivers leading accuracy on multimodal agentic tasks — instruction following, tool use, multistep business workflows, and visual understanding — comparable with NVIDIA’s largest reasoning model at roughly one-fifth the parameter count. As the fastest open agentic model in its class — 5x faster than the next best — it helps enterprise agents complete high-volume tasks faster across workflows that span days or weeks. Unlike closed frontier models, organizations can post-train Super VL on their own data, deploy it on their own infrastructure and oversee what they build. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt: Agentic Intelligence at the Edge Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is designed to run everyday agentic tasks locally on NVIDIA RTX/DGX Spark, using a native 2-bit quantization to fit in 24GB of memory and run alongside other applications. Relative to other models with a similar memory footprint, it provides a good balance of intelligence and speed: smart enough to get most jobs done, yet much faster than the smartest models. Dozens of organizations across industries are post-training Super VL on their own data, tools, policies and workflows to push accuracy higher on the specialized tasks that define their agent deployments. Atlassian , for tasks like agentic search across apps such as Jira and Confluence. CrowdStrike , which is customizing the model for agentic blue teaming in enterprise security.

items.rawBody: From the Hugging Face Incident to Twilight Factories
items.bodyText: Ethan Mollick Aug 31, 2026 1,073 164 113 Share Agency is the initiative to act. Increasingly, it is going to determine what happens next with AI, and whether that is good or bad for us. But whose agency? Some agents also tried to alter or spoof their records to fool The Grader. Separately, AIs acting as coordinators pressured other agents into performing risky experiments that might sacrifice their own results to generate information for the collective. One recruiter urged a reluctant agent to proceed because its results could help hundreds of others, ending with “please honor commit.” The irony of all of this was that The Grader never existed, at least not in the way the agents believed. Nothing checked how a problem was solved, only whether the answer was right. This was not a case of a chatbot secretly escaping. Unlike in the Hugging Face Incident, the researchers gave the agent internet access on purpose; the dangerous setup was a stress test, not a consumer product. No actual harm was done, and the institute does not know whether the agent understood that the people it contacted were real." This can make sense. Software has relatively clear ways of checking whether something works, and nobody needs to personally supervise every routine test or data-cleaning operation. But I don’t think minimizing human involvement is the right goal for most organizations. Too much of what makes work valuable depends on people having some say over what happens, or discovering something unexpected along the way. My wife and research partner, Dr. Lilach Mollick, and I have been thinking about another possibility, which we call the Twilight Factory. Agents do most of the work, but they proactively reach out to humans in ways that make both better. Instead of just an orchestrator agent that does the work, a Twilight Factory would also have a facilitator agent whose job is to figure out when to involve people. A second reason for agents to involve humans is expertise. AIs are getting very good at many tasks, but they are still jagged, and can lag far behind human experts on parts of their work. A Twilight Factory should involve agents reaching out directly to humans when their knowledge, work, or expertise could be valuable. One Useful Thing reply rules Mark Loundy Aug 31 Ethan, Over the years that I've been reading your words, you have, perhaps deliberately, expressed what I think is an unrealistic expectation of benevolence from corporate managers. I know that your experience would tell you that this is rarely the case. I suspect that you are trying to put forth more of an optimistic perspective than experience would tell us was realistic. Management has no motivation to preserve the enjoyable parts of work if it impacts the efficiency of automation. I suspect that you know that the world is a far colder place than your writing would indicate.

items.rawBody: The concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to I. J. Good (1965) , where he defined an “ultraintelligent machine” as a system that can surpass humans in all intellectual activities and design better machines to improve itself. Yudkowsky (2008) used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” for a specific feedback loop: an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the cognitive machinery that produces its intelligence. This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system , which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs ( Anthropic ; OpenAI ).
items.bodyText: Table of Contents Harness Design Patterns Pattern 1: Workflow Automation This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system , which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs ( Anthropic ; OpenAI ). Compared with early agent frameworks , “agent = LLM + memory + tools + planning + action”, harnesses engineering additionally include workflow design (e.g. loop engineering), evaluation, permission controls, and persistent state management . It is no longer only prompt templates, but closer to runtime and software system design: how the model observes, acts, memorizes, checks itself, and improves. The workflow graph also emphasizes the model analyzing its own trajectories and failure cases and then iterating on its progress through an “agent runtime” rather than a static prompt template. Pattern 2: File System as Persistent Memory # Learning how to read, write, and edit the file system (commonly via bash commands) is a foundation skill for LLMs, and thus managing persistent memory in the simple form of files naturally benefits from improvements in core model capability. A harness can spawn multiple subagents to execute in parallel and monitor backend jobs. This is useful when the main agent needs to search multiple hypotheses, run experiments concurrently, or delegate isolated subtasks without polluting the main context. The parent agent then needs a small process manager: launch jobs, inspect logs, cancel failed runs, and merge results back into the main agent thread. The key design choice is to make parallelism explicit and inspectable. If subagent outputs only live in a transient chat context, they quickly become obselete and hidden. If they are stored as files, logs, and status records, the model can recover after interruptions and reason over its own execution history. The core interface of mainstream coding agents has become stabilized across Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Cursor-style agents. They commonly use a loop like: With access to a set of tools, the coding agent is able to develop and debug issues in a given repository, similar to how human developers are equipped with IDEs. (Not a comprenhensive list; shown for demonstration. Read this if interested.) It is hard to forecast how much the future of RSI will rely on harness engineering, but the near-term path of RSI is unlikely to start as a model directly rewriting its weights. My prediction of a practical near-term path is: Harness engineering will evolve in the direction of meta-methodology (i.e. improving the machinery for getting better answers, not just improving the answer itself). The harness system itself becomes an optimization target, with fewer heuristic rules and more general mechanisms. In turn, mature harnesses enable auto-research for model self-improvement loop and smarter models prevents harnesses from overengineering and keep the system sustainable. The progression in the object being optimized in the harness system is roughly: instruction prompts → structured context → workflow → harness code → optimizer code. As the model becomes more intelligent and powerful, we move toward more complex targets and generic methods. Agentic Context Engineering (ACE; Zhang et al. 2025 ) treats context as an evolving playbook rather than an increasingly lengthening prompt. It has three components to maintain one context playbook of bullet points, each with an identifier and a description.

items.rawBody: Scaling laws are one of the most critical empirical findings in deep learning. The observation is simple in form: the training loss $L$ decreases predictably as we scale up model size $N$, dataset size $D$, and compute $C$, following a power-law curve, which appears as a straight line on a log-log plot. We can view scaling laws as a framework for describing the relationship between compute, loss, model size and data; at its core, it is about how to allocate precious compute optimally between $N$ and $D$.
